sections.title: Welcome to the Windmill Experience!
sections.preview: Get ready to step into the past. This tour leads you through a restored island village, the windmiller's daily life, and a few hidden stories from the 1940s.
details: Get ready to step into the past. You will not need a time machine for this journey, just some comfy shoes.

Thanks to the beautiful restoration by the Voudouris family, you can see how islanders lived more than a century ago, long before Wi-Fi was even invented. You will also uncover some secret history from the 1940s.
Today, you get to walk in the shoes of a real windmiller. His daily workout routine included lifting heavy sacks of flour all day to help feed most of the village.

items.label: The giant windmill
items.text: Explore a real working windmill from the bottom all the way to the top.

items.label: Village life
items.text: Peek inside the traditional house and the bakery.

items.label: Nature and animals
items.text: Sniff the wonderful herbs in the gardens, visit the threshing floor, and say hello to the donkeys.

items.label: Underground secrets
items.text: Walk through a real military tunnel connected with the 1940s.

details.text: How to listen to the tour

details: The QR code opens the tour from the beginning. Choose your language, turn up your phone's volume or share headphones, and follow the numbers around the village.
Move forward to our gardens with herbs.

items.text: Take your special Mylotopi Sketch and colored pencils with you.
Keep your eyes wide open as you walk around the windmill, heavy stones, and old tools.
Try to remember the beautiful colors you see so you can turn your drawing into a masterpiece at the restaurant-cafe.

sections.title: Our Garden with Our Herbs!
sections.preview: Take a deep breath. These gardens smell like an outdoor kitchen and a village pharmacy at the same time.
details: Take a deep breath. Does it smell like a giant outdoor kitchen or a village pharmacy? Actually, it is both.
Before modern medicine and supermarkets, these gardens were an island survival kit. These plots are filled with the same kinds of herbs that have grown here for centuries.

Herbs like thyme, oregano, and marjoram were not only used to make dinner taste amazing. They were also the local doctor. If someone had a stomach ache, the windmiller's family would come here to pick leaves for a natural remedy.
Look at the purple lavender and bright green mint. They look as if someone painted them into the garden, so pay close attention to those colors.
Once your nose is happy, follow the scent of the sea breeze toward the historic windmill.

items.text: Put the phones away for a moment and look for the physical puzzle pieces.
Use your eyes and your nose to figure out which word belongs to which plant.
Give the leaves a tiny, gentle rub and sniff, but please do not eat the garden before lunch.
Can you tell the difference between mint and oregano? Which one smells like pizza, and which one smells like a cozy nap?
Remember the greens, greys, and purples for your Mylotopi Sketch later.

sections.title: The Windmill Base (1st Floor)
sections.preview: Step inside the Mill of the Priest, the oldest working windmill on Kos and in the Dodecanese complex.
details: Welcome to the Mill of the Priest. You are standing inside the oldest working windmill on the entire island and in the whole Dodecanese complex.
It is more than 400 years old, operated daily until 1987, and is still a living machine that grinds flour today.
As you step through the doorway, notice the traditional pomegranate hanging for good luck, alongside a small bottle of Holy Water from Mount Athos that is more than 9 years old.
This giant machine is 6.2 meters tall, and the stone walls around you are 1.2 meters thick to keep the building safe from wild sea storms.
On the higher floors, there are two massive grinding stones that weigh one ton each. Together, they weigh more than two tons.
About 80% of the wood in this building is original, and the rest was brought from Mount Athos. Some of the reused wooden parts above are between 1,000 and 1,300 years old.

items.label: To your right
items.text: The area covered with a rag was the miller's storage room. Nearby you can see a wooden donkey saddle, a threshing sledge, everyday wooden tools, and photos of other windmills across Greece.

items.label: The fireplace
items.text: The miller did not use it only for warmth. The can inside held cow fat, which was melted to lubricate the moving parts of the windmill.

items.label: Kostas Politis
items.text: Above the fireplace is a photograph of the beloved owner of this windmill, whose legacy lives on here.

items.label: To your left
items.text: A traditional scale and weights were used to weigh the fresh flour carefully.

items.label: The first brakes
items.text: The tiny rope hanging down was the windmill's first braking system. The miller pulled it to lift the two-ton millstones just enough to make it safe to go outside and unwrap the sails.

details: Move forward to the second floor of the windmill.

items.text: Stand next to the doorway and stretch your arms as wide as you can. Are your arms longer than the wall is thick, or does the windmill win?
Look around the room and see if you can spot the wooden donkey saddle.
Peer into the fireplace. Can you spot the hidden can of cow fat?
Find the tiny hanging rope that acted as the windmill's braking system.

sections.title: The Windmill Sleeping Area (2nd Floor)
sections.preview: The second floor reveals a surprise: this working windmill was also where the windmiller and his family slept.
details: Welcome to the second floor. Watch your step on the wooden stairs and mind your head on the wood above.
On the walls to your right, you will see pictures showing historic windmills from across Greece. But this space was not only a gallery.

Here on the right side is where the windmiller and his entire family used to sleep. Imagine trying to take a peaceful nap while the building was shaking, the wind was howling, and heavy machinery was crushing wheat nearby.
Now look to the left side. This was a very important and busy storage space.

The miller used this side of the room to stack heavy bags of raw wheat waiting to be ground, alongside freshly filled bags of white flour ready to feed the village. He kept them near his bed so he could protect them.
Move forward to the third floor of the windmill.

items.text: Could you imagine yourself sleeping on the second floor exactly as the windmiller's family used to do?

sections.title: The Windmill Machinery (3rd Floor)
sections.preview: At the top of the windmill, the beams, stones, ropes, brakes, and sails show how wind became flour.
details: Welcome to the third floor. Please watch your step on the ladder and mind your head as you explore.
You are now looking at the real power of the windmill. The massive wooden beam above the stones is the main connector linking the heavy stones inside, the gears, and the giant spinning sails outside.
The grinding stones weigh more than two tons together. They were imported from Nisyros, an island famous for producing a unique, super-strong stone perfect for milling.

items.label: The feeder and bell
items.text: Above the stones is a wooden box called the feeder, where the miller poured the raw wheat. A tiny bell rang when the wheat ran low so he knew it was time to refill it.

items.label: The first brake
items.text: A wooden lever connected to a tiny rope links down to the first floor and works with the braking system you saw below.

items.label: Dropping the flour
items.text: Near the lever is a trap door connected to a pipe. When the flour was ready, it dropped straight down to the bottom floor.

items.label: The miller's tip
items.text: A second, smaller trap door let the miller keep a small percentage of the flour as payment for his hard work.

items.label: Smooth spinning
items.text: Near the trap doors is a little can. Upstairs, the miller used a mixture of olive oil and soap to keep the upper gears running smoothly.

items.label: Emergency brake
items.text: The thick rope near the ladder was the second braking system, used when the miller needed to stop making flour quickly.

items.label: A ship's ceiling
items.text: Look up at the ceiling. It is designed in the shape of a ship to enhance the power of the mechanism and produce flour more quickly.

details: Move forward to the threshing floor and the donkeys area.

items.text: Can you find the tiny bell that warned the miller when the wheat was running out?
Can you ring it?
Scan the floor and see if you can spot the special tip door where the miller kept his hard-earned payment.

sections.title: Threshing Floor & the Donkeys!
sections.preview: Back outside, the round stone threshing floor shows how crops were prepared before wheat reached the mill.
details: Welcome back outside. Take a deep breath of fresh air.
You are now standing near the traditional threshing floor, which looks a lot like a big, round stone dance floor.
Look in the middle of the circle at the wooden post. In the old days, the miller loosely tied a rope from that post around a donkey's neck.
The donkey walked round and round in a big circle, using its heavy feet to stomp and smash the harvested crops so the seeds could break free.

After the hardworking donkey did all this dizzy stomping, the miller carefully separated the white wheat from the brown wheat. Today, this method is no longer used here; wheat is bought directly from local producers on the island.
You do not just have to imagine the animals. Nearby you can meet the real stars of the farm: two lovely donkeys.

items.label: Melina
items.text: The proud mama donkey is 6 years old.

items.label: Katie
items.text: Her sweet little daughter is just 2 years old.

items.label: Katie's dad
items.text: Nobody actually knows where he went. He loved to sing loudly, so perhaps he walked to the next town to start a donkey rock band.

details: Move forward to the cellar and Italian tunnel.

items.text: Step up to the edge of the threshing floor and pretend you are attached to the center wooden post.
Can you walk in a perfect circle just like a donkey did?
After your dizzy dance, wave hello to Melina and Katie from a distance.
Please do not put your fingers near the donkeys. They look sweet, but they might mistake fingers for baby carrots.

sections.title: The Secret Tunnel & Cellar
sections.preview: Step underground into a cooler, quieter space where wine, stone, and World War II history meet.
details: Prepare for a total change of scenery as we head underground. As you step down into the cool air, look to your left and right.

You will see rows of local wine from the Skevofilax winery in Kos. These bottles are displayed here for design; the wines for drinking are kept safely in the main cellar, where the temperature is right for them.
Back in the 1940s, during World War II, this space was not for wine. It was for survival.
This 20-meter tunnel was built by Italian soldiers during the war. They used it as a hurry tunnel, a secret shortcut to run away and hide from their opponents.
The cellar itself was used as a safe shelter where soldiers could sleep, relax, and stay protected from battles outside.
At the end of the tunnel, you come out into our backyard, which is now our peaceful restaurant. Before you exit, look back at the stone roof.
In the 1940s, this whole area was a shooting range. The top was covered in heavy stone to protect the soldiers, and at the edge they had a machine gun position to defend the hillside.
It is hard to believe this quiet, beautiful spot for a meal was once a heavily guarded place on the island.
When you finish exploring the tunnel, come back and find our tour guide so they can show you the way to the traditional house and the bakery.

items.text: As you walk through the soldiers' tunnel, can you calculate exactly how many bottles of wine line the walls?

sections.title: The Traditional House
sections.preview: This tiny home is over 130 years old and shows how 8 to 10 family members could share less than 20 square meters.
details: Welcome to the traditional house. This amazing little home is more than 130 years old.
It measures less than 20 square meters, but 8 to 10 people used to live here: grandparents, parents, and all the children in one single room.
The grandparents slept by the warm fireplace. The parents slept high in the loft bed on the opposite side, while older children slept in the beds next to it and on the couch.
What about the baby? Look for the little wooden cradle. Someone could gently pull the hanging rope to rock the baby to sleep.
Notice the space underneath the family beds. That was their main storage room.

items.label: Daily chores and decor
items.text: On the left side, you can see a large wooden loom used to make new clothes and repair old ones, alongside a chest for personal items.

items.label: Flour and memory
items.text: You will also spot a sifter used for flour, beautiful old photographs, and religious pictures on the walls.

items.label: Vases and uniforms
items.text: Next to the chest are two vases: the large one was for wine, and the small one was for water. Above them hang traditional uniforms worn by the ladies of the house for weddings and special events.

items.label: The heart of the home
items.text: The fireplace was used to cook meals and keep the family warm. Nearby are a small hand-grinder mill, daily kitchenware, and traditional plates decorated with painted flowers.

items.label: The hanging swing
items.text: Look up at the ceiling. The hanging object that looks like a swing was not for playing. Fresh bread was kept in the top part, safely away from mice, while carobs were stored in the bottom part.

items.label: A traditional refrigerator
items.text: The wooden cabinet has two parts. Ice cubes went in the top, and as the ice melted, the family could open a small tap to drink cold water. The cold also chilled the lower section to keep food fresh.

details: Move forward to the bakery.

items.text: Can you find the hand-grinder mill? Try putting the wooden handle into the gap and see if you can spin it around.
Can you spot the hanging swing that kept bread away from mice?
Can you find the tiny rope they pulled to rock the baby to sleep?
Imagine what it would be like to share this small room with 8 to 10 family members.

sections.title: The Bakery
sections.preview: The traditional stone oven is more than 150 years old and tells the story of daily bread, shared work, and village life.
details: Welcome to the traditional oven. This beautiful stone oven is more than 150 years old.
Back in the day, most of the ladies in the village came here to bake daily bread for their families.
Baking bread was not as fast as running to the supermarket. It was a two-day process.
The night before, the ladies carefully mixed and shaped the dough, leaving it to rest and rise overnight.
The next morning, when the dough was ready, they built a hot fire to warm the oven. Once the temperature was just right, they placed the dough inside.
After one to two hours of baking, the whole village filled with the delicious smell of fresh, warm bread ready to be eaten.
Look around and you can see photographs showing how this whole procedure was done.
Now it is time to head to the restaurant-cafe. Grab your colored pencils, enjoy a well-deserved snack, and finish making your Mylotopi Sketch a colorful masterpiece.
Thank you for exploring with us today.

items.text: The whole village needed fresh bread. Can you guess what time the baker had to wake up every morning to start making the dough?
Hint: it was long before the sun came up.
Take a close look at the pictures to see how the village ladies used to work in the bakery.
